title: Data Modeling: Is Normalization Still Relevant?
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
During my university days (in the 90s), we studied relational databases as the gold standard of data modeling, applying normal forms from 1NF to 3NF and beyond—normalization was the ultimate goal. Yet, in over 30 years of working with SQL databases, I’ve heard less talk about those normal forms and more about denormalization, which developers reach for as soon as they encounter performance issues. Fast-forward to today: as I work with MongoDB, a NoSQL database, I’m hearing about third normal form (3NF) all over again. Ironically, many of the same developers who once couldn’t wait to denormalize their tables now cite normalization, often as a way to avoid learning a different modeling approach: domain-driven design and document data modeling. Let's examine the goals of normalization from the perspective of modern software development.

Normalization for Casual End-Users—But What About Developers?

Let's review the original papers to gain a better understanding of the motivations for normalization and see how they apply to modern applications. E. F. Codd’s 1971 paper, Normalized Database Structure: A Brief Tutorial, describes six objectives of normalization. But first, take a look at how the paper begins. The abstract states:

Casual and other users of large formatted data bases need a simple tabular (relational) view of the data rather than a network or tree-structured view. This paper illustrates the removal of repeating groups, hierarchic and plex structures, and cross-referencing structures. Finally, the simplification of data base relations by normalization is discussed.

This is directly relevant to normalization and document databases: a document model is hierarchical, embedding sub-objects and arrays (so-called “repeating groups”), or similar to a network model when referencing other documents by their "_id". Precisely what the relational model was designed to replace. However, are you a "casual user" of the database, as described in this paper? Relational databases and SQL were initially intended for non-programmers, allowing end-users to connect directly through a command line. Humans could write commands to define data structures (DDL) and manipulate data (DML) in an English-like syntax, without needing to learn a procedural language full of loops and variables.

Codd further explains his intent:

To make formatted data bases readily accessible to users (especially casual users) who have little or no training in programming we must provide the simplest possible data structures and almost natural language.

Suppose you are a non-programmer sitting in front of an IBM 3270 green-screen text terminal. The relational model is designed for you. You benefit from viewing tables as two-dimensional grids rather than as hierarchical structures of nested documents and references. When reading data, you want to query logical structures without needing to understand how the data is stored. When updating, you want to avoid making changes in multiple places, which risks accidental inconsistency. When entities need to change structure, you want to avoid pointers and references that can break other parts of the system. If more data arrives, you hope storage and structure are no hurdle. Normalization, as we’ll see, was designed to meet these goals—improving the database user experience, especially for non-programmers. SQL itself was based on this vision: an English-like language for both data manipulation (DML) and data structure (DDL).

Of course, these features still aid DBAs and users working with reporting tools. SQL will never die, and all databases must provide an SQL interface for ad-hoc queries, but what about applications? Today, as a developer, you work with procedural or object-oriented languages, mapping business entities to interconnected objects, such as aggregates in Domain-Driven Design, with well-understood access patterns. You want to control execution in your code, rather than analyze database execution plans when problems arise. Your application objects define a data structure with their access methods. As data types evolve and use cases change, updating your application code is routine, whereas applying DDL changes to the database often requires separate tools and teams. Let's examine the goals of normalization and their relationship to modern application development more closely.

Codd’s Six Reasons for Normalizing

In Normalized Database Structure: A Brief Tutorial, E.F. Codd introduces normalization and outlines six main benefits. These are grouped differently below, according to later publications, and quoted directly from the paper with their original numbering.

Two fundamental reasons for normalization

Codd emphasizes two main goals—agility and consistency, which are essential even before considering normal forms.

  • Agility: Reduce the need for restructuring as new data types appear

4) To reduce the need for restructuring the collection of relations as new types of data are introduced, and thus increase the life span of application programs;

By normalizing and decoupling data, it becomes easier to evolve the data model—adding a column to one table doesn’t force changes elsewhere. This supported flexibility before “agile” was popularized. Document models offer even more flexibility, as fields can vary between documents (polymorphism).

  • Consistency: Reduce undesired insertion, update, and deletion dependencies:

3) To free the collection of relations from undesirable insertion, update and deletion dependencies;

With normalized models, data duplication is minimized, reducing the risk of inconsistency. Originally, databases were operated by non-programmer end-users, who could easily forget to update all copies of duplicated data. Today, updates are made by developers through code, which is planned, reviewed, and tested, partially shifting where and how consistency is enforced. With a document model, consistency is built into the application code and follows the same development, testing, and deployment process as the application.

Two reasons to transform to the first normal form (1NF)

Among the remaining reasons, two are closely associated with First Normal Form.

  • Visualization: Make it feasible to present data as two-dimensional tables:

1) To make it feasible to tabulate any relation in the data base;

In the early days, this meant avoiding repeating groups in columns, such as arrays or nested tables. On mainframes and early PC applications, data was shown in simple text grids. There were no modern GUIs with drill-down features to explore hierarchical or network structures. Today, reading nested JSON documents or clicking on links can be easier for developers than joining multiple relational tables. Modern applications handle object graphs, often with attributes as Arrays or Lists. Normalizing these into multiple tables requires complex queries with many joins or complex object-relational mapping (ORM) and ambiguous fetch strategies (lazy N+1 or eager reading too much). A document model avoids the intermediate table format and skips the ORM transformations between the database and application objects.

  • Querying: Provide a powerful retrieval capability:

2) To obtain a powerful retrieval capability by means of a simpler collection of relational operations than would otherwise be necessary;

Normalized models enabled the use of declarative query languages, such as SQL, which appeared later, representing a significant improvement over procedural data access. While programmers of the past appreciated abstracting away procedural logic, today’s developers often prefer to control data access directly in their application code, including iterating and shaping data as needed in their programming language of choice, and optimizing physical storage to colocate data that is accessed together. A document model offers similar retrieval capabilities, particularly through MongoDB's aggregation pipelines, which chain set-based operations, much like SQL subqueries or common table expressions (CTE), but supporting nested objects and arrays.

Two reasons to consider higher normal forms (2NF and 3NF)

The last two benefits of normalization touch on model clarity and query independence.

  • Self-Documenting: Make the model more informative to users:

5) To make the relational model more informative to users;

One logical model with decoupled entities and relationships could be printed and pinned on the office wall for everyone to see. All applications in the enterprise used this normalized model, and all teams had to synchronize on it when the applications evolved. Today, this same clarity is often achieved by splitting systems into distinct domains, each with its database and ownership (as in Domain-Driven Design). A domain model consists of interconnected objects that include both behavior and data. A document model is tailored for workloads within a particular domain and maintains the same ubiquitous language used by users, developers, and data modelers. The interface with other domains is decoupled through a dedicated application API or event streaming, rather than sharing a common database. The model is documented in the application code (annotated objects) rather than an in-database catalog.

  • Workload Independent: Make the model neutral to query statistics:

6) To make the collection of relations neutral to the query statistics, where these statistics are liable to change as time goes by.

Codd aimed to create schemas that avoided embedding assumptions about queries or usage, allowing the model to remain independent of specific access patterns or data sizes. Today, it is uncommon to design a database schema without understanding the application that will access it. With the increasing number of applications and data, the era of a single, monolithic database for all enterprise applications has passed. The traditional waterfall approach, where data structures are defined before application functions, is incompatible with shorter release cycles. When utilizing a document data model, it is crucial to choose wisely between embedding and referencing, avoiding unbounded arrays, and identifying whether workloads are read-heavy or write-heavy.

I categorized the objectives into three groups: agility for schema evolution, first normal form to prevent repeating groups, and higher normalization for independence from workload. In Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model, Codd identifies two of these as the basis, which refer to agility and workload independence:

a basis for protecting users of formatted data systems from the potentially disruptive changes in data representation caused by growth in the variety of data types in the data base and by statistical changes in the transaction or request traffic

Ironically, these same goals helped drive the rise of NoSQL databases, such as MongoDB, which feature flexible data schemas and elastic infrastructure, with polymorphism and sharding, and without relying on normal forms. What changed so dramatically? Two major shifts:

  • First, the primary "users" of databases are now object-oriented application programs rather than end-users running ad-hoc queries. SQL is used as an API for the persistence layer, rather than a language dedicated to database-centric processing.
  • Second, release cycles have decreased from years to weeks, demanding faster adaptation and giving development teams more independence within smaller business units. Domain-Driven Design enables teams to develop and deliver software with greater autonomy, eliminating the need for coordination with other development or operations teams.

Please note that this approach isn't mandatory, and an RDBMS is still the best choice for creating a large, centralized database supporting multiple applications via PL/SQL stored procedures. However, such monolithic systems are now rare or considered legacy. When normalization for multiple applications isn't required, adopting a document model can greatly simplify the system. Keeping it simple benefits other aspects as well: faster development, more reliable deployment, and improved performance.

It’s Your Development Organization That Dictates the Model

A common misconception is that the data itself dictates the modeling method (I've heard claims that "my data is relational", or "my data is JSON"). In Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model, Codd makes it clear that normalization is about how data is described, not data itself. The same information can be represented using either a normalized relational schema or alternative structures, such as a document or nested model, with query equivalence across normal forms. The main difference lies in query complexity and how the schema, without code or comments, is self-documenting of the structure:

Although the three normal forms are query equivalent in the sense that the set of queries answerable by a collection C in first normal form is transformable into queries yielding the same information from the second and third normal forms of C, there is a difference in information content of the three forms. The second is more informative than the first, and the third is more informative than the second. The increased information lies in the data description (rather than in the data described) as a consequence of the underlying conventions.

You can choose between a relational and a document model, and both are suitable for your application queries. Other models, such as graph databases, are also possible, but those without a schema, like key-value stores, may not meet the goal of being informative to users. A document model is more than just a flat set of key-value pairs. MongoDB organizes data into sub-objects and arrays, similar to tables in a relational model. MongoDB provides schema validation, enabling you to define the structure of your data with specific data types, rules, and descriptions. It's essential to consider this when storing documents in SQL databases with a JSON datatype that lacks schema validation and has limited indexing options for sub-objects or arrays. In a document database, documents should be the native storage format, not an added datatype to a row- or column-based store.

For any application, you can opt for either a relational or a document database model, but your developer experience might vary. Using a monolithic database with a predefined schema—designed before analyzing application use cases—tends to favor a normalized model. When developing a database for a domain where the main access patterns are well-defined, normalization is a feasible approach. However, normalization may introduce unnecessary complexity in object-relational mapping, whereas a document model is often more straightforward.

When Normalization Is More Trouble Than It’s Worth

In Further Normalization of the Data Base Relational Model, Codd acknowledged that strict normalization can sometimes be costly or unfeasible. As normal forms may not be necessary for domain-driven data modeling, I'll list these cases to clarify when normalization may cause trouble.

1. Schema Changes (“Attribute Migration”) impact applications

Attribute migration can logically impair an application program… the re-interpretation is likely to cause significant system overhead. Avoidance of attribute migration is accordingly desirable.

Codd mentions two ways to mitigate this impact: "avoid insertion and deletion on the relations affected by attribute migration" and "casting the database in third normal form at the earliest possible time." In practice, this premature optimization will make the data model too complex when it is not needed, such as considering all relationships as many-to-many, just in case the business evolves in that direction. In MongoDB, this is easier as one document may have a different schema than another one in the same collection (polymorphism), and a field can be a scalar in one document and an array in another.

2. Referential Integrity: More “Admissible States” to Manage and Enforce

The schema for B2 permits insertions and deletions not permitted by the schema for B1. It is accordingly reasonable to say that these schemata are not insertion-deletion equivalent.

Codd explains that a higher normal form is more permissive and can accommodate data that lower forms cannot, which is why referential integrity constraints, such as foreign keys, have been introduced to prevent inconsistent data. Embedding a one-to-many relationship directly within a document model, rather than normalizing it into separate documents with references, naturally enforces some integrity constraints. This approach is similar to using ON DELETE CASCADE with foreign keys, but avoids the associated performance penalty.

3. Not All Transitive Dependencies Can Be Eliminated

It is not always possible to remove all transitive dependencies without losing information.

There are some cases where the 3NF cannot be applied even if the 2NF still has transitive dependencies. Understanding those cases is difficult, and simply allowing dependencies within a document can make the model simpler. Application functions need to ensure these dependencies are preserved during updates, but most data in modern databases is not frequently updated because they must retain temporal information.

4. Original Target Was the Enterprise-Wide Shared Database

For the large integrated data bases of the future, application-independent guidelines for logical record design are sorely needed.

Codd’s normalization is crucial for designing large, shared databases for unknown applications, ensuring data consistency, reducing redundancy, and allowing flexibility. However, for specific business domains with known access patterns, strict normalization can add unnecessary complexity and performance issues. In such cases, a more practical, domain-driven approach — sometimes involving controlled denormalization — often results in more straightforward and efficient solutions tailored to the specific needs.

Normalization Objectives Matter More Than Normal Forms

Looking back at the origins of normalization, it’s clear that its purpose was never to be an absolute law, but rather a set of strategies to address specific challenges faced by users of large, shared databases—especially those with changing requirements and diverse applications. Today, developers, not end-users, drive database design, and applications often take the lead, with databases built to support their needs.

Modern development focuses on flexibility, speed, and team autonomy. Database schemas now follow agile, object-oriented practices, giving developers control over structure and evolution alongside code. Data modeling practices are less about enabling enterprise-wide ad hoc queries and more about meeting current application and organizational needs. For domain-driven, fast-changing applications, strict normalization can introduce unnecessary complexity and slow down the process. If your data structure does not need to be application-agnostic or built before knowing your access patterns, a document data model can be a more straightforward and adaptable approach.
